newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico railway bid profitable in 2 yrs - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico railway bid profitable in 2 yrs - analysts.

text.p: Cheaper labor costs should help make Mexico's Northeast Railway concession profitable after two years of operation, Bear Stearns analysts Santiago Pique and Marc McCarthy wrote in a report.

Mexico's Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM) and Kansas City Southern Industries, through joint venture Transportacion Ferroviaria Mexicana (TFM), won a 50-year concession in December, bidding $1.4 billion to operate the key trade route.
"We calculate that TFM (as a stand-alone operation) should become profitable in its second year of operations, and should become free-cash-flow positive by the third year," the report said.
TFM is expected to halve the present work force and enjoy higher margins than U.S. counterparts because of lower labor costs, the analysts said.

"The government must dismiss every employee and accept all of the labor liabilities prior to selling the concession. TFM will then hire the personnel it requires to operate the business, which we estimate to be approximately 4,100 employees, less than half the current number," the report said.

While analysts were concerned the concession's unexpectedly high price tag would dilute short-term earnings, Pique and McCarthy wrote that the Northeast railway should surpass typical U.S. railroad margins after the first year of operations.

The Bear Stearns report said average operating margin for six U.S railways is 20 percent, compared to the brokerage's estimates for the concession of 25 percent after the first year and 45 percent in five years.
"The average cost of a Mexican railroad worker is approximately three times the minimum wage, an amount that represents 20 percent of the comparable U.S. cost of labor," the analysts wrote.
The government recently agreed to repurchase a temporary $237.5 million equity stake in the railway, which it will pay when TFM makes its final railway payment before July 31.
